notes.meaning: During the Passover meal, Jesus took bread, thanked God, broke it into pieces, and gave it to His disciples. He told them to eat it, explaining that the broken bread represents His body, which was about to be given and broken for them on the cross. Just as ordinary bread gives life to the body, trusting in Christ gives spiritual life to the soul.

differ.view: Believers do not feed on Christ's physical body, but Christ is truly and spiritually present to nourish the souls of those who take the bread by faith.
The bread is a visual symbol and memorial to help believers remember the Lord's physical death until He returns.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The bread changes completely in its hidden substance into the actual physical body, blood, soul, and divinity of Jesus, keeping only the outer appearance of bread.

notes.meaning: Jesus next took a cup of wine, offered a prayer of thanksgiving to God, and passed it to the disciples. He specifically told all of them to drink from it. Sharing the one cup showed their common share in the blessings He was about to purchase for them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The whole Christ is fully present in each element, so church members receive all the spiritual blessings of the sacrament even when receiving only the bread.

notes.meaning: Jesus explained that the wine represents His own blood, which seals the new covenant, or solemn agreement between God and humanity. Under the old agreement, animal blood was sprinkled to cover sin, but Jesus poured out His own life once for all people so their sins could be forgiven.

Jesus announced that this would be His last meal with them before His death. He looked ahead past the cross to the joy of heaven, where He will celebrate a greater banquet together with all His redeemed people in the Father's kingdom.

Before leaving the room, Jesus and His disciples joined together in singing a hymn, which was traditionally the group of praise songs from Psalms 113 to 118. Even with His deepest sufferings directly ahead, Jesus sang praises to God before walking out into the night toward the Mount of Olives.

Jesus warned the disciples that within hours, every one of them would stumble and run away in fear because of what would happen to Him. He showed them this was not an accident, but the fulfillment of the Old Testament prophecy in Zechariah, where the shepherd is struck down and the sheep are scattered.

Jesus immediately gave them comfort by promising that death would not be the end. After rising from the dead, He would go ahead of them to Galilee like a shepherd leading His flock, gathering His scattered followers back together.

Peter boldly spoke up and insisted that even if every other disciple deserted Jesus, he never would. Though Peter truly loved Jesus, he relied on his own human willpower and thought he was braver than his fellow disciples.
Jesus gave Peter a direct, solemn warning about his coming failure. He told Peter that before the rooster crowed early the next morning, he would disown Jesus three separate times.

Refusing to accept the Lord's warning, Peter doubled down, claiming he would choose to die with Jesus rather than deny Him. Caught up in the moment, all the other disciples promised the exact same thing, unaware of how weak they really were.

Jesus brought His followers to Gethsemane, an olive grove with an oil press at the base of the Mount of Olives. He instructed eight of the disciples to sit down and rest while He walked a little farther into the grove to pray alone.

Jesus took His closest three companions—Peter, James, and John—deeper into the garden. As He walked with them, an intense, crushing grief and anguish began to overwhelm His soul as He faced the full weight of the sins He was about to carry.

Jesus openly shared His inner anguish with the three, telling them that His grief was heavy enough to kill Him. He asked them to stay in that spot and keep awake with Him, desiring their companionship and spiritual support in His darkest hour.

Jesus went a short distance ahead, threw Himself facedown on the ground, and pleaded with His Father. He asked if there was any possible way for this bitter cup of suffering and divine judgment against sin to be taken away, yet He completely yielded His own human feelings to the Father's plan.

When Jesus returned to the three disciples, He found them fast asleep instead of praying. He addressed Peter directly, gently asking if he could not keep watch and stay awake with his Master for even one single hour after making such bold promises.

Jesus urged them to stay alert and pray so they would not give in when sudden trials tested their loyalty. He kindly acknowledged that their inner desires were good and sincere, but their physical human nature was frail and easily overcome.

Jesus withdrew a second time to pray, this time expressing complete acceptance of the cross. Recognizing that the redemption of sinners could happen in no other way, He prayed that the Father's purpose would be carried out, whatever the cost.

Returning once more, Jesus found His disciples asleep again because deep grief and exhaustion had made their eyelids heavy. Knowing their weakness, He left them resting, went back to His place of prayer, and cried out to the Father a third time with the same heartfelt words.

Coming back the final time, Jesus told the disciples that their time to watch and rest had run out because the decisive hour had arrived. With full resolve gained through prayer, He commanded them to stand up, not to run away, but to walk directly forward to meet the one who was betraying Him.

While Jesus was still speaking, Judas stepped into view leading a large mob sent by the ruling Jewish council. The crowd was carrying torches, swords, and wooden clubs, coming armed as if they were setting out to capture a violent criminal.

To make sure the guards did not grab the wrong person in the dark, Judas had arranged a preplanned signal to point Jesus out. He walked straight up to Jesus, greeted Him with the respectful title of Teacher, and kissed Him warmly under the guise of friendship.

Jesus calmly addressed Judas as a companion and told him to carry out what he had come to do, exposing the betrayal while showing no malice. At that moment, the armed men rushed in, grabbed hold of Jesus, and placed Him under arrest.
